# 👋 Today’s Goals

By the end of today, you will be able to:

- Explain what “data” means in analytics  
- Identify different forms of data (structured, unstructured, semi-structured)  
- Understand what tables, rows, columns, observations, and variables are  
- Describe what a **dataframe** is in R  
- Distinguish numerical, categorical, **nominal vs. ordinal**, date, and factor types  
- Recognize common data quality issues  
- Begin inspecting data in R

# 📦 What Is Data?

**Simple definition:** Data = recorded information.

Data comes in many forms:

- Numbers  
- Text  
- Images  
- Video  
- Audio  
- Clicks  
- Sensors  
- Transactions  
- Social interactions  

---

# 🧭 Types of Data in the Real World

| Type | Structure | Examples | Where you see it |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Structured** | Rows + columns | Spreadsheets, CSVs, SQL tables | Finance reports, gradebooks |
| **Semi-Structured** | Tagged but irregular | JSON, XML, API payloads | Web services, mobile apps |
| **Unstructured** | No fixed schema | Images, text, video, audio | Social media, sensors |

> We will live primarily in the **structured** column this semester, but you will see hints of the others in APIs/shiny dashboards later.

---

# 📊 Why Focus on Tabular Data?

- Most analytics → spreadsheets, reporting tables, dashboards  
- Easiest way to learn logic of data manipulation  
- R and tidyverse are built around tabular workflows  
- Models require clean, clearly defined variables  
- Visualization becomes easier and more useful  

---

# 🧱 What Is a Dataset?

A dataset is a **collection of observations**.

Each dataset contains:   
- **Rows** → individual observations     
- **Columns** → variables or attributes     
- **Cells** → values  

---

# 📐 Anatomy of a Table

```text
| player_id | home_arena | season_score | role    |
|-----------|------------|--------------|---------|
| P-0041    | Neon Yard  | 780          | Striker |
| P-0199    | Glow Hall  | 655          | Anchor  |
| P-0112    | Glow Hall  | NA           | Scout   |
```

- **Rows** = single player
- **Columns** = attributes we measure
- **Cells** = individual facts (may be missing!)

---

# 📁 What Is a “Dataframe” in R?

A **dataframe** is R’s way of storing tabular data.

- Each column = one variable  
- Each column has **one type**  
- Rows represent observations  
- Foundation for almost all analysis  

```r
ENIA_ROOT <- "~/ENIA-5120"
players <- readr::read_csv(file.path(ENIA_ROOT, "data", "laser_league_players.csv"))

class(players)
dplyr::glimpse(players)
summary(players$season_score)
```

```text
[1] "spec_tbl_df" "tbl_df"      "tbl"         "data.frame"
Rows: 100
Columns: 11
$ player_id        <chr> "P-0001", "P-0002", ...
$ role             <chr> "Striker", "Anchor", ...
$ season_score     <dbl> 720, 655, NA, 590, ...
$ tag_accuracy_pct <dbl> 78.2, 70.5, 65.1, ...
$ assists          <dbl> 120, 98, 88, 73, ...
   Min. 1st Qu. Median Mean 3rd Qu. Max.
  320     520     610   612    705   890
```

- Internally, a dataframe is a **list of equal-length vectors**.
- Keeping types consistent (character vs numeric) prevents silent bugs later.

---

# 🧩 Common Variable Types (Laser League examples)

| Type | What it looks like | Example column |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Numeric (continuous)** | Counts, rates | `season_score`, `assists`, `tag_accuracy_pct` |
| **Numeric (discrete)** | Whole numbers | `matches_played` |
| **Categorical (nominal)** | Names/labels | `home_arena`, `preferred_loadout` |
| **Categorical (ordinal)** | Ordered labels | `skill_tier` (Bronze < Silver < Gold) |
| **Logical** | TRUE/FALSE flags | `injured_flag` |
| **Date / time** | Calendar stamps | `last_match_date` |
| **Factor** | Encoded categorical (R) | `role` as factor for modeling |

---

# 🔠 Nominal vs. Ordinal (Important!)

| Type | Example | Visual cue |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Nominal** (unordered) | `home_arena` = {Neon Yard, Glow Hall, Photon Dome} | 🔹 Neon | 🔸 Glow | 🔺 Photon (reorder any way) |
| **Ordinal** (ordered) | `skill_tier` = {Rookie < Veteran < Elite} | Rookie → Veteran → Elite |

- Nominal categories are labels; order never matters.
- Ordinal categories imply ranking; keep sequences when encoding factors.
- Be precise: mixing these up causes broken summaries and misleading models.

---

# ⚠️ Data Quality Issues to Watch

- Missing values (e.g., some players have no `season_score`)
- Duplicated IDs after data entry
- Weird casing (`neon yard` vs `Neon Yard`)
- Impossible numbers (negative assists?)  
- Inconsistent categories (`Anchor` vs `anchor`)
- Timestamps saved as text

We will practice spotting these issues in Lab 01 and fix them systematically in later sessions.

---

# 👀 Quick R Demo (Live)

```r
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

ENIA_ROOT <- "~/ENIA-5120"
players <- readr::read_csv(file.path(ENIA_ROOT, "data", "laser_league_players.csv"))

players %>%
  count(role) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = role, y = n, fill = role)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Players by role", x = NULL, y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()
```

- We preview the data, build a quick count plot, and save it as `role_plot`
- This pattern is key for initial data analysis (read → inspect → visualize)

```text
# A tibble: 4 × 2
  role     n
  <chr> <int>
1 Anchor   27
2 Scout    25
3 Striker  24
4 Support  24
```
---

- Visualize it immediately to reinforce the habit.

```{r role-plot, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.cap="Example role distribution (Laser League data)", fig.width=6.5, fig.height=3.5}
library(ggplot2)
library(tibble)
role_counts <- tibble(
  role = c("Anchor", "Scout", "Striker", "Support"),
  n = c(27, 25, 24, 24)
)

ggplot(role_counts, aes(x = role, y = n, fill = role)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Players by role (example)", x = NULL, y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)
```

- The column chart mirrors this summary; we can talk through which roles dominate.

---

# 🧠 Why Variable Types Matter

- Encodes how R treats the column (math vs. grouping vs. dates)
- Drives visualization defaults (continuous vs. discrete scales)
- Impacts modeling formulas (factors vs. numeric)
- Avoids silent bugs like “ZIP codes minus ZIP codes”

Use `glimpse()` or `dplyr::count(where(is.character))` to sanity check types the moment you read in data.

---

# 🧹 Understanding Common Data Problems

Data gets messy because of:

- Manual entry & typos  
- Multiple systems exporting data differently  
- Missing context (optional survey fields)  
- Copy/paste casing differences  
- Merge errors that duplicate IDs  
- Sensors or loggers dropping packets  

We will turn these into learning opportunities in labs.

---

# ⚠️ Typical Problems You Will Encounter

| Issue | Laser League example | Quick check |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Missing values** | `season_score` empty for new recruits | `colSums(is.na(players))` |
| **Outliers** | Accuracy = 150% (impossible) | `summary(players$tag_accuracy_pct)` |
| **Wrong type** | `last_match_date` stored as text | `lubridate::ymd(last_match_date)` |
| **Inconsistent labels** | `neon yard` vs `Neon Yard` | `count(players, home_arena)` |
| **Duplicates** | Same `player_id` twice after merge | `duplicated(players$player_id)` |

---

# 🔍 Detecting Problems in R

```r
players %>%
  summarise(
    missing_score = sum(is.na(season_score)),
    bad_accuracy = sum(tag_accuracy_pct > 100 | tag_accuracy_pct < 0),
    unique_arenas = dplyr::n_distinct(home_arena)
  )

players %>%
  count(home_arena) %>%
  arrange(desc(n))
```

- Quick summaries expose anomalies immediately
- Save these checks in your labs → earns rubric points for reproducibility
